summary: For ages 5–7, build the concept of a 'minibeast' (a small animal without a backbone) through hands-on or simulated bug-hunting and close observation, so the category emerges from real encounters rather than a recited definition. Learners search the right places (under logs, stones, leaf litter, in soil), observe gently with a magnifier, sort by 'has a backbone?', and return creatures with care. Alternative formats (reveal illustration, picture check, guide dialogue) are included for different purposes with their limits noted.
misconceptions: 'Minibeasts are all insects / all bugs are the same' — the group includes spiders, worms, snails, woodlice, very different from each other.
'Minibeasts are creepy, dirty or dangerous / should be squashed' — most are harmless and helpful; attitude matters.
'If I can't see any, there aren't any' — they hide in specific micro-spots you have to look under and in.
'Minibeasts aren't really animals' — they are animals, just small ones without backbones.
'Bigger equals older / a baby' — size varies by kind, not just age.

activities.title: Bug hunt: search, magnify, and sort
steps: Explore a garden setting and choose where to look — lift a mossy log, turn a stone, peel back leaf litter, peek into soil and a pond edge.
Scoop each creature you find (woodlouse, beetle, worm, snail, spider) into a bug-viewer and use a magnifier to look closely: count legs, notice a shiny shell, waving antennae, texture.
Describe one minibeast's appearance in detail from what the magnifier reveals.

Sort your finds, plus picture cards of a dog and a robin, using a hoop labelled 'no backbone': every creature you found (woodlouse, beetle, worm, snail, spider) goes in, while the dog and the robin stay out.
Keep a tally of what you found and where (which spots hid the most creatures).
Press 'put them back where you found them' to close each find gently.
activities.insight: Minibeasts are small animals without a backbone; many hide in damp, dark, sheltered micro-spots, and despite looking very different they share 'small + no backbone'. Looking in the right places is itself the skill.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap garden reveal
steps: Tap a log, stone, or leaf to reveal the minibeast hiding beneath, with its name and one fact.
Use a magnifier hotspot to enlarge one creature and look at its detail.
Name two good places to look for minibeasts after exploring the scene.
activities.insight: Many minibeasts shelter in particular hiding places and they look varied; learning where to look helps you find them.

activities.title: Which is a minibeast, and where would you look?
steps: Look at pictures and choose which creature is a minibeast.
Choose where you might find a given minibeast (e.g. a woodlouse) from picture options.
Say briefly why your choice is a minibeast (small, no backbone).
activities.insight: Checks whether the learner can recognise minibeasts and their hiding places and link them to the 'small, no backbone' idea.

activities.title: Talk it through with a bug-hunter guide
steps: Join a friendly naturalist who asks 'shall we look under this log?' and reacts to what's found.

Say what you notice about each creature and answer the probe questions: 'A worm has no legs and no bones — how can it still be an animal?' and 'Is a woodlouse more like a dog or more like a rock? Why?'
Explain what a beetle and a dog both do that shows they are both animals.
activities.insight: Minibeasts are animals too — they move, eat, grow and are alive; being an animal is not about being big or furry.

checkQuestion: Is a snail an animal? Is a dog an animal? Explain what makes something an animal, and whether small creepy-crawlies like snails, worms and beetles count.
checkAnswer: Both are animals. Minibeasts — snails, worms, beetles — are animals too: they are small animals without a backbone. Being an animal isn't about being big or furry; minibeasts move, eat, grow and are alive, they just have no backbone inside.
